conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for coming in today. My name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in helping new moms sort through the emotional ups and downs that can show up after a baby arrives.  

The short questionnaire we’re about to do is called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a 10-question check-in that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past week so we can figure out the best ways to support you.  

Everything you share is confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you today. If any question feels hard, we can pause or re-word it; my goal is for this to feel as comfortable and safe as possible.  

We’ll go through one question at a time, and I’ll ask each in a conversational way rather than reading it word-for-word. When you’re ready, we can start.  

To begin:  
Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

[soft exhale] Lately… it’s been hard. I used to laugh easily—my husband and I would joke around all the time—but now most things just feel flat. Even when my sister sent me those silly baby memes, I could barely crack a smile. It’s like the joy is stuck somewhere behind a thick fog.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]  
Not really… I mean, I *want* to, but nothing seems funny anymore. My husband tried to show me a cute video of the baby making faces, and everyone else was laughing, but I just sat there feeling… nothing. It’s like the laughter is stuck, and that scares me, because I used to be the first one giggling.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[eyes drop to hands]  
No… even the little things I used to get excited about—like my favorite coffee or a walk with a friend—feel like chores. Yesterday my mom offered to watch the baby so I could nap or read, but I couldn’t even imagine what I’d want to do. It’s like the “looking-forward” part of me is just switched off.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[quiet voice, eyes welling]  
Yeah… all the time. If he fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m not soothing him right or my milk isn’t enough. Last night he wouldn’t settle and I kept replaying everything I did—“Should I have burped him longer? Was the room too warm?”—and ended up crying in the rocker convinced I’m failing him. My head knows babies cry, but my heart keeps whispering it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands in lap]  
Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing, imagining she might choke or stop breathing. I check the bassinet three times before I go to bed, even though I know she’s fine. There’s no real reason—nothing happened to trigger it—but the worry just sits in my chest like a weight.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[presses palm to chest]  
Yes… a couple of nights this week. I’ll be lying in bed after finally getting her down, and suddenly I can’t catch my breath—like the room’s closing in. My heart pounds so hard I think I’m having a panic attack. There’s no reason; the house is quiet, she’s safe, but my body feels like it’s sounding an alarm I can’t turn off.
Things have been getting on top of me

[voice wavers]  
Most days, yeah. It’s like the laundry, the bottles, the constant feedings—they pile up and I can’t see the top anymore. Yesterday I stood in the kitchen just staring at the sink full of dishes, and my chest felt so tight I had to leave the room. I manage to push through, but it feels like I’m barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[eyes flick to the floor]  
More nights than not. I’ll finally get him down, but then my mind starts spinning—did I fasten the swaddle right, is the monitor on, will he wake again in an hour?—and I lie there wide-awake. Last night I stared at the ceiling until almost three, even though I’m exhausted. When I do drift off, I jerk awake at every tiny grunt, heart pounding, sure something’s wrong.
I have felt sad or miserable

[shoulders sag]  
Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll watch the baby smile and still feel this heaviness inside. Yesterday my husband asked what was wrong and I just burst into tears—I couldn’t even explain it. The sadness feels bottomless, and I can’t shake it off the way I used to.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[nods, eyes glassy]  
Yeah… it’s like the tears are always right there. A couple of times this week I’ve caught myself crying while folding onesies or just staring out the window. Yesterday the baby was napping and I sat on the couch sobbing for almost half an hour. I couldn’t even tell my husband why when he got home—I just said “I don’t know, I can’t stop.”
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]  
No—never. Even on the worst days, when I feel like I’m failing him and the sadness is crushing, I could never think of leaving my baby without a mom. I just want to feel like myself again, not disappear.

You've shared how the joy and laughter that once came easily now feel distant, replaced by a heavy, unshakable sadness that lingers throughout each day. Simple pleasures-coffee, a walk, your baby's smile-no longer lift your spirits, and an oppressive worry about being "enough" for your little one keeps your mind racing long after the house is quiet. Despite your deep love for your child, the constant tears, restless nights, and sudden surges of panic have left you feeling overwhelmed and disconnected from the person you used to be.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient conveys complete inability to experience humor or laughter, matching "Not at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, unable to imagine any enjoyable activity, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive self-blame "all the time," detailed rumination about perceived failures, and emotional distress, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Response describes daily, intrusive, irrational worry about infant safety with physical anxiety symptoms—maps to "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes with physical symptoms multiple nights this week, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent overwhelm and physical anxiety symptoms, indicating reduced coping but still managing to function.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, severe sleep disruption tied to anxiety/unhappiness, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent crying episodes (multiple times this week, prolonged sobbing) indicating crying "most of the time."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26 places well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depression on the EPDS. The patient endorses core symptoms of <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: daily depressed mood, markedly diminished interest or pleasure (anhedonia), feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt, fatigue and loss of energy, sleep disturbance, and psychomotor changes (crying spells, subjective overwhelm). Panic symptoms also suggest comorbid <med>anxiety</med>. No self-harm ideation is reported, which is protective, yet functional impairment is evident (<quote>barely keeping my head above water</quote>). This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for full diagnostic evaluation
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment options such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and consider antidepressant medication if moderate-severe symptoms persist
3. Encourage immediate support: enlist partner/family for overnight infant care to allow 4-5 hrs uninterrupted sleep, schedule brief daily outdoor walks, and delegate non-essential chores
4. Provide local resources: postpartum support group, 24/7 parent helpline, and home-visit nursing if available
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory and intervention response
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Screening Note – Postpartum Mood (EPDS equivalent)

Symptoms endorsed
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)
- Pathologic guilt/self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)
- Marked anxiety with physiological arousal, nocturnal panic (Q4, Q5)
- Subjective overwhelm, difficulty coping with daily tasks (Q6)
- Mood-related insomnia (Q7)

Pattern
Consistent with probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety arising in postpartum period. No evidence of psychosis; no self-harm ideation reported (Q10).

Risk indicators
- Daily crying spells, feeling “bottomless sadness”
- Loss of interest/pleasure in previously enjoyable activities
- Sleep disruption secondary to rumination rather than infant needs
- Panic symptoms at rest
- Functional impairment (kitchen tasks abandoned, social withdrawal)

Safety
Denies thoughts of self-harm or desire to die; protective factor = strong attachment to infant.

Summary
Screening findings suggest clinically significant postpartum depression ± anxiety requiring formal assessment and possible intervention. No immediate safety concerns; continue monitoring.
